claim: Men continue to hold most tenured and leadership positions in STEMM fields despite efforts to increase gender diversity.
source: Despite efforts to increase gender diversity in science, technology, engineering, mathematics and medicine (STEMM), men continue to hold most tenured and leadership positions.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the abstract without specific data citation, but is supported by data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Male overrepresentation and related gender-based advantages are rarely mentioned in conversations about gender equality.
source: however, male overrepresentation and related gender-based advantages are rarely mentioned in conversations about gender equality.
evidence: This is an observational claim about discourse patterns in the field.

claim: Gender bias exists in the citation of scientific papers.
source: For example, studies have reported gender bias in the citation of scientific papers (Larivière et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Larivière et al., 2013.

claim: Gender bias exists in assessments of the scientific quality of abstracts submitted to conferences.
source: in assessments of the scientific quality of abstracts submitted to conferences (Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2013.

claim: Gender bias exists in the language used for letters of recommendation.
source: in the language used for letters of recommendation (Trix and Psenka, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Trix and Psenka, 2003.

claim: Gender bias exists in teaching evaluations.
source: in teaching evaluations (MacNell et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to MacNell et al., 2015.

claim: The number of women accessing higher education has tripled globally in the last 30 years.
source: Although the number of women accessing higher education has tripled globally in the last 30 years
evidence: This statement is followed by citations to Hurtado, 2021 and UNESCO, 2021 in the next clause.

claim: There are still more men than women in academic positions in science and medicine.
source: there are still more men than women in academic positions in science and medicine (Hurtado, 2021; UNESCO International Institute for Higher Education in Latin America and the Caribbean, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurtado, 2021 and UNESCO, 2021.

claim: Women and men receive many advanced degrees, such as MDs and PhDs in the biomedical sciences, in roughly equal numbers.
source: despite women and men receiving many advanced degrees, such as MDs and PhDs in the biomedical sciences, in roughly equal numbers (Beeler et al., 2019; Llorens et al., 2021; Salinas and Bagni, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Beeler et al., 2019; Llorens et al., 2021; Salinas and Bagni, 2017.

claim: As of 2018, only 25% of full professors in academic medicine in the United States were women.
source: For example, as of 2018, only 25% of full professors and 19% of department chairs in academic medicine in the United States (US) were women, as opposed to 75% and 81% of men in these positions, respectively (AAMC, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to AAMC, 2020 data.

claim: As of 2018, 75% of full professors in academic medicine in the United States were men.
source: For example, as of 2018, only 25% of full professors and 19% of department chairs in academic medicine in the United States (US) were women, as opposed to 75% and 81% of men in these positions, respectively (AAMC, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to AAMC, 2020 data.

claim: As of 2018, only 19% of department chairs in academic medicine in the United States were women.
source: For example, as of 2018, only 25% of full professors and 19% of department chairs in academic medicine in the United States (US) were women, as opposed to 75% and 81% of men in these positions, respectively (AAMC, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to AAMC, 2020 data.

claim: As of 2018, 81% of department chairs in academic medicine in the United States were men.
source: For example, as of 2018, only 25% of full professors and 19% of department chairs in academic medicine in the United States (US) were women, as opposed to 75% and 81% of men in these positions, respectively (AAMC, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to AAMC, 2020 data.

claim: The gender ratios in US academic medicine roughly parallel those of NIH staff researchers with tenured positions (23% women, 77% men).
source: These ratios roughly parallel those of NIH staff researchers with tenured positions (23% women, 77% men) and tenured faculty in the European Union (21% women, 79% men) (NIH Gender Inequality Task Force Report, 2016; Salinas and Bagni, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to NIH Gender Inequality Task Force Report, 2016 and Salinas and Bagni, 2017.

claim: The gender ratios in US academic medicine roughly parallel those of tenured faculty in the European Union (21% women, 79% men).
source: These ratios roughly parallel those of NIH staff researchers with tenured positions (23% women, 77% men) and tenured faculty in the European Union (21% women, 79% men) (NIH Gender Inequality Task Force Report, 2016; Salinas and Bagni, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to NIH Gender Inequality Task Force Report, 2016 and Salinas and Bagni, 2017.

claim: If the rate of progress over the last decade is maintained, gender parity at the full professor level in academic medicine in the US will not be reached until 2054.
source: indeed, if the rate of progress over the last decade is maintained, we will not reach gender parity at the full professor level in academic medicine in the US until 2054, and it will be 2063 before there is parity at the department chair level (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: Based on linear projections from 2009-2018 AAMC data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: If the rate of progress over the last decade is maintained, gender parity at the department chair level in academic medicine in the US will not be reached until 2063.
source: indeed, if the rate of progress over the last decade is maintained, we will not reach gender parity at the full professor level in academic medicine in the US until 2054, and it will be 2063 before there is parity at the department chair level (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: Based on linear projections from 2009-2018 AAMC data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 80 world leaders pledged at a United Nations summit in 2015 to end gender discrimination by 2030.
source: This slow rate of progress would also fall well short of the pledge made by 80 world leaders at a United Nations summit in 2015 to end gender discrimination by 2030, including the commitment of "reaching parity for women at all levels of decision-making" (UN Women, 2015; UN Women, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to UN Women, 2015 and UN Women, 2016.

claim: The UN summit pledge included a commitment to reaching parity for women at all levels of decision-making.
source: This slow rate of progress would also fall well short of the pledge made by 80 world leaders at a United Nations summit in 2015 to end gender discrimination by 2030, including the commitment of "reaching parity for women at all levels of decision-making" (UN Women, 2015; UN Women, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to UN Women, 2015 and UN Women, 2016.

claim: In 2018, there were 38,767 full professor positions in US medical schools.
source: In 2018, three-quarters of the 38,767 full professors in US medical schools were men.
evidence: Specific numerical data from AAMC, 2020.

claim: In 2018, three-quarters of full professors in US medical schools were men.
source: In 2018, three-quarters of the 38,767 full professors in US medical schools were men.
evidence: Specific numerical data from AAMC, 2020.

claim: If the total number of full professor positions remains constant, the fraction of women in these positions needs to double to achieve gender parity.
source: If the total number of full professor positions remains constant, the fraction of women in these positions needs to double, and the fraction of men needs to be reduced by one third, to achieve gender parity (Figure 1C)
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: If the total number of full professor positions remains constant, the fraction of men needs to be reduced by one third to achieve gender parity.
source: If the total number of full professor positions remains constant, the fraction of women in these positions needs to double, and the fraction of men needs to be reduced by one third, to achieve gender parity (Figure 1C)
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: If the number of male full professors remains constant, an additional 19,156 full professor positions would be needed to achieve gender parity.
source: Alternatively, if the total number of full professor positions is increased to allow the number of female professors to be doubled, without changing the number of male professors, an additional 19,156 new positions will be needed to achieve gender parity (Figure 1C)
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of faculty positions in science and engineering fields has essentially remained constant over the last 30 years.
source: This latter scenario would require a substantial increase in overall resources and would contrast with trends from the last 30 years showing that the number of faculty positions in science and engineering fields has essentially remained constant (Schillebeeckx et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schillebeeckx et al., 2013.

claim: In 2018, there were 3,292 department chair positions in US medical schools.
source: For department chair positions (which numbered 3,292 in 2018), if the total number remains constant, the number of women needs to increase by a factor of 2.5 (from 639 to 1,646) to reach parity
evidence: Specific numerical data from AAMC, 2020.

claim: If the total number of department chair positions remains constant, the number of women needs to increase by a factor of 2.5 (from 639 to 1,646) to reach parity.
source: For department chair positions (which numbered 3,292 in 2018), if the total number remains constant, the number of women needs to increase by a factor of 2.5 (from 639 to 1,646) to reach parity
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on 2018 data.

claim: Achieving gender parity in department chair positions while keeping the total number constant would involve just over one thousand male department chairs being replaced by women.
source: this would involve just over one thousand male department chairs being replaced by women (Figure 1D)
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Achieving gender parity in department chair positions by increasing the number of positions would require 2,014 new positions.
source: Alternatively, achieving parity by increasing the number of positions would require 2,014 new positions (Figure 1D)
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At the assistant professor level, 54% of posts are held by men and 46% by women.
source: While the situation is better at the assistant professor level, where 54% of posts are held by men and 46% by women
evidence: Specific numerical data from AAMC, 2020.

claim: Men experience lower rates of sexual harassment than women in STEMM fields.
source: For example, men experience lower rates of sexual harassment than women (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2018.

claim: Identical curriculum vitae have been reviewed more favorably when the applicant was thought to be a man.
source: Moreover, identical curriculum vitae have been reviewed more favorably (by both male and female science faculty) and considered for higher starting salaries when the applicant was thought to be a man, suggesting that men are also given more credit than women for identical achievements (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss-Racusin et al., 2012.

claim: Identical curriculum vitae have been considered for higher starting salaries when the applicant was thought to be a man.
source: Moreover, identical curriculum vitae have been reviewed more favorably (by both male and female science faculty) and considered for higher starting salaries when the applicant was thought to be a man, suggesting that men are also given more credit than women for identical achievements (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss-Racusin et al., 2012.

claim: Both male and female science faculty review identical curriculum vitae more favorably when the applicant was thought to be a man.
source: Moreover, identical curriculum vitae have been reviewed more favorably (by both male and female science faculty) and considered for higher starting salaries when the applicant was thought to be a man, suggesting that men are also given more credit than women for identical achievements (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss-Racusin et al., 2012.

claim: Men are given more credit than women for identical achievements.
source: Moreover, identical curriculum vitae have been reviewed more favorably (by both male and female science faculty) and considered for higher starting salaries when the applicant was thought to be a man, suggesting that men are also given more credit than women for identical achievements (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CV study cited (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012).

claim: Small advantages or disadvantages can have large cumulative effects over time.
source: Studies have shown that even small advantages or disadvantages can have large cumulative effects over time.
evidence: Supported by the workplace simulation study cited in the following sentences.

claim: Valuing the performance of a male employee at just 3% above the performance of a female employee resulted in a shorter trajectory for the male employee to reach an executive level.
source: As one workplace simulation demonstrated, valuing the performance of a male employee at just 3% above the performance of a female employee resulted in a shorter trajectory for the male employee to reach an executive level, with half the number of successful projects required. This was sufficient to generate substantial male overrepresentation and female underrepresentation at executive levels (Du et al., 2021; Nordell, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Du et al., 2021 and Nordell, 2021.

claim: A 3% performance valuation advantage for male employees resulted in male employees requiring half the number of successful projects to reach executive level compared to female employees.
source: As one workplace simulation demonstrated, valuing the performance of a male employee at just 3% above the performance of a female employee resulted in a shorter trajectory for the male employee to reach an executive level, with half the number of successful projects required. This was sufficient to generate substantial male overrepresentation and female underrepresentation at executive levels (Du et al., 2021; Nordell, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Du et al., 2021 and Nordell, 2021.

claim: A 3% performance valuation advantage for male employees was sufficient to generate substantial male overrepresentation and female underrepresentation at executive levels.
source: As one workplace simulation demonstrated, valuing the performance of a male employee at just 3% above the performance of a female employee resulted in a shorter trajectory for the male employee to reach an executive level, with half the number of successful projects required. This was sufficient to generate substantial male overrepresentation and female underrepresentation at executive levels (Du et al., 2021; Nordell, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Du et al., 2021 and Nordell, 2021.

claim: The self-serving bias refers to the tendency to attribute one's own success to internal factors and one's failures to external ones.
source: The self-serving bias refers to the tendency to attribute one's own success to internal factors and one's failures to external ones (Miller and Ross, 1975; Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller and Ross, 1975 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: The self-serving bias is considered to be an important component of adaptive function and mental health.
source: While this bias is considered to be an important component of adaptive function and mental health, it may also cause people to perceive themselves being better than others, and negatively impact negotiation processes (Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997; Gelfand et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997 and Gelfand et al., 2002.

claim: The self-serving bias may cause people to perceive themselves being better than others.
source: While this bias is considered to be an important component of adaptive function and mental health, it may also cause people to perceive themselves being better than others, and negatively impact negotiation processes (Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997; Gelfand et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997 and Gelfand et al., 2002.

claim: The self-serving bias may negatively impact negotiation processes.
source: While this bias is considered to be an important component of adaptive function and mental health, it may also cause people to perceive themselves being better than others, and negatively impact negotiation processes (Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997; Gelfand et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997 and Gelfand et al., 2002.

claim: 85% of men surveyed by AAMC thought their institute offered equal opportunities to faculty regardless of gender.
source: When the American Association of Medical Colleges (AAMC) examined perceptions of equality they found that 85% of men surveyed thought their institute "offered equal opportunities to faculty regardless of gender", which raises the question of what factors the respondents attributed to the significant gender disparities at their institutes (AAMC, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to AAMC, 2020.

claim: Participants in the 'Athena SWAN Charter for Women in Science' reported resentment of what mostly male respondents viewed as positive discrimination.
source: Analyses of experiences and perceptions of participants in the 'Athena SWAN Charter for Women in Science' reported resentment of what mostly male respondents viewed as positive discrimination – that women were suddenly receiving external advantages, such as faster promotion timelines or new positions created specifically for women, and that this was both unfair and anathema to equality (Ovseiko et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ovseiko et al., 2017.

claim: Male respondents in the Athena SWAN Charter viewed faster promotion timelines for women as unfair and anathema to equality.
source: Analyses of experiences and perceptions of participants in the 'Athena SWAN Charter for Women in Science' reported resentment of what mostly male respondents viewed as positive discrimination – that women were suddenly receiving external advantages, such as faster promotion timelines or new positions created specifically for women, and that this was both unfair and anathema to equality (Ovseiko et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ovseiko et al., 2017.

claim: Male respondents in the Athena SWAN Charter viewed new positions created specifically for women as unfair and anathema to equality.
source: Analyses of experiences and perceptions of participants in the 'Athena SWAN Charter for Women in Science' reported resentment of what mostly male respondents viewed as positive discrimination – that women were suddenly receiving external advantages, such as faster promotion timelines or new positions created specifically for women, and that this was both unfair and anathema to equality (Ovseiko et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ovseiko et al., 2017.

claim: Educating participants about self-serving bias and requiring them to delineate weaknesses in their own position had a positive impact on the negotiation process in settlement negotiations.
source: One study of settlement negotiations in a mock trial showed that educating participants about self-serving bias and requiring them to delineate weaknesses in their own position had a positive impact on the negotiation process, suggesting there is room to intercede (Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to Babcock and Loewenstein, 1997.

claim: Men are proportionally far less burdened than women when it comes to performing the work required for gender equality initiatives.
source: Finally, when it comes to performing the work required for gender equality initiatives, such as committee activities, data collection and documentation, men are proportionally far less burdened than women (Caffrey et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Caffrey et al., 2016.

claim: The Initiative on Women in Science and Engineering from the New York Stem Cell Foundation piloted a report card for gender equality.
source: The Initiative on Women in Science and Engineering from the New York Stem Cell Foundation piloted a report card for gender equality, which evaluates an institute's commitment to promoting gender equality (Beeler et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Beeler et al., 2019.

claim: The report card for gender equality evaluates an institute's commitment to promoting gender equality.
source: The Initiative on Women in Science and Engineering from the New York Stem Cell Foundation piloted a report card for gender equality, which evaluates an institute's commitment to promoting gender equality (Beeler et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Beeler et al., 2019.

claim: Simply increasing the number of women in leadership is unlikely to be sufficient to achieve gender parity.
source: It is important to note that gender disparity has many causes, and that simply increasing the number of women in leadership is unlikely to be sufficient to achieve parity.
evidence: This is a reasoned inference based on the complexity of gender disparity causes.

claim: As the number of women in tenured and leadership positions increases, the number of men holding these positions will need to decrease, or alternative models of power and leadership will need to be implemented.
source: As the number of women in tenured and leadership positions increases, the number of men holding these positions will need to decrease, or alternative models of power and leadership will need to be implemented.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mathematics of achieving parity.

claim: In a highly competitive system, the disadvantages of one group advantage others and vice versa.
source: In a highly competitive system, the disadvantages of one group advantage others and vice versa.
evidence: This is a logical inference about competitive systems.

claim: In STEMM fields, men benefit both from fewer of the disadvantages faced by women and from direct advantages.
source: In STEMM fields, men benefit both from fewer of the disadvantages faced by women and from direct advantages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the evidence of gender bias and disparities presented.

claim: Conversations about inequalities in STEMM fields often use men as the reference point.
source: Conversations about inequalities in STEMM fields often use men as the reference point, highlighting the underrepresentation and disadvantage of women relative to men.
evidence: This is an observational claim about discourse patterns.

claim: Discussions around gender-based advantages for men at each career stage are far less common than discussions of gender-based disadvantages for women.
source: If one were to ask a group of women in STEMM fields to discuss gender-based disadvantages, one would likely hear numerous examples of career obstacles and instances of bias, discrimination and/or harassment faced by women. By contrast, discussions around gender-based advantages for men at each career stage are far less common.
evidence: This is an observational claim about discourse patterns.

claim: Focusing solely on the underrepresentation and disadvantage of women may contribute to the illusion that men are simply a neutral reference point.
source: Focusing solely on the underrepresentation and disadvantage of women may contribute to the illusion that men are simply a neutral reference point.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the effects of discourse framing.

claim: The self-serving bias may influence perceptions of advantage and could be used to justify current gender disparities and resist equality initiatives.
source: Similar to the myth of meritocracy, the self-serving bias may influence perceptions of advantage and could be used to justify current gender disparities and resist equality initiatives, if not corrected.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential effects of self-serving bias.

claim: Reductions in long-standing advantages could be mistaken for disadvantages if they are not acknowledged in the first place.
source: Reductions in long-standing advantages, such as shorter promotion timelines or receiving more credit for equal work, could also be mistaken for disadvantages if they are not acknowledged in the first place.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about perception of advantage reduction.

claim: Acknowledging the many external factors accelerating academic career success is particularly important, given their unequal distribution between genders.
source: Acknowledging the many external factors accelerating academic career success is particularly important, given their unequal distribution between genders (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a normative claim supported by the evidence of unequal external factors shown in Figure 2.

claim: The STEMM community's understanding of male advantage may influence the strategies used to address gender equality.
source: Practically speaking, the STEMM community's understanding of male advantage may influence the strategies used to address gender equality, such as giving women explicit advantages versus removing known obstacles.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about how understanding affects strategy.

claim: Gender equality work may further disadvantage women with workloads that are not part of their career advancement.
source: This may further disadvantage women with workloads that are not part of their career advancement and reinforce the perception that gender inequality is an issue that only impacts women and therefore needs to be solved by women.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of unequal distribution of equality work.

claim: Unequal distribution of gender equality work may reinforce the perception that gender inequality is an issue that only impacts women and therefore needs to be solved by women.
source: This may further disadvantage women with workloads that are not part of their career advancement and reinforce the perception that gender inequality is an issue that only impacts women and therefore needs to be solved by women.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of unequal distribution of equality work.

claim: Gender disparities have become smaller over the last decade.
source: Although gender disparities have become smaller over the last decade, progress has been slow
evidence: This is supported by the data trends shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Progress toward gender parity has been slow over the last decade.
source: Although gender disparities have become smaller over the last decade, progress has been slow
evidence: This is supported by the data trends and projections shown in Figure 1.

claim: The current rate of progress toward gender parity would fall well short of the UN pledge to end gender discrimination by 2030.
source: This slow rate of progress would also fall well short of the pledge made by 80 world leaders at a United Nations summit in 2015 to end gender discrimination by 2030
evidence: This is an inference based on the projected timelines (2054 and 2063) compared to the 2030 target.

claim: There are two paths to achieving gender parity: increasing the number of women while reducing the number of men, or increasing the number of women without reducing the number of men.
source: There are essentially two paths to achieving parity: increasing the number of women in these positions while reducing the number of men, or increasing the number of women without reducing the number of men.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the mathematical possibilities for achieving parity.

claim: To maintain 38,767 full professor positions, the number of women would need to increase by approximately 9,590 and the number of men would need to decrease by approximately 9,566 to achieve parity.
source: To maintain 38,767 full professor positions (the number in 2018, including 23 with gender unreported), the number of women would need to increase by approximately 9,590 (from 9,794–19,384) and the number of men would need to decrease by approximately 9,566 (from 28,950–19,384).
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: To maintain 3,292 department chair positions, the number of women would need to increase by 1,007 and the number of men would need to decrease by 1,007 to achieve parity.
source: To maintain 3,292 department chair positions (the number in 2018), the number of women would need to increase by 1,007 (from 639 to 1,646) and the number of men would need to decrease by 1,007 (from 2,653–1,646).
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on 2018 data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Achieving parity by increasing positions without reducing male department chairs would likely require a new model of departmental leadership.
source: This latter scenario would likely require a new model of departmental leadership, such as a system with co-chairs of departments or rotating department chairs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about what would be needed to accommodate more positions.

claim: Circumstances unique to each institution or field will need to be considered to ensure gender parity throughout the career stages.
source: Moreover, circumstances unique to each institution or field, such as the early-career pipeline, promotion timelines and retention rates of women and men, will need to be considered to ensure gender parity throughout the career stages.
evidence: This is a normative claim about what should be done.
